title: Investigating the effects of sub-surface microstructure within crystal plasticity
abstract: Abstract Safe operation is vital in the nuclear industry. This is achieved through codes and standards that incorporate overly conservative assumptions. Reducing these over-conservative assumptions, whilst maintaining confidence in the results, could lead to increased plant lifetime and so increased production of low carbon energy. Material models, such as crystal plasticity finite element (CPFE) methods, may improve the predictions of codes and standards because they account for microstructural effects directly. For industry to adopt CPFE as a material modelling method, it must be sufficiently validated. One area that is difficult to validate is the effect of sub-surface microstructure on mechanical response due to the complexity associated with acquiring it. This study explores the impact of sub-surface microstructure on CPFE modelling, primarily focusing on deformation. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) is combined with serial sectioning using a focused ion beam to collect a 3D representation of the microstructure below the surface. The microstructure collected is implemented into a CPFE model and compared with a simulation that does not consider the sub-surface microstructure. The intragranular elastic strain and local orientation changes are compared to experimental data. Difference between results is seen, with the inclusion of sub-surface microstructure leading to closer agreement with EBSD data. Graphical abstract

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Prediction of component lifetime within nuclear reactor power plants remains an important area of research due to its safety critical nature. Current standards for this field are dictated by macro-scale continuum modelling approaches, which are unable to directly account for mesoscale microstructural effects [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. This often leads to overly conservative estimates of remaining life, and as such means that components are removed from service before it is necessary.

To tackle this shortcoming of current standards, the crystal plasticity finite element (CPFE) method can be utilized to directly account for microstructure and other mesoscale phenomena. This is because it has been shown by [ 4 ] that by accounting for the microstructure through such models, a more accurate prediction of material response can be achieved.

Whilst CP has been an area of significant research over the past 40 years [ 5 ], it is still of great interest and has potential to improve our understanding of material behaviour. To ensure any CP model developed is a realistic prediction of material behaviour, it is necessary to validate said model. Many different forms of validation have been proposed; from comparing lattice reorientation using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) data [ 6 ], to directly measuring strain fields with high-resolution digital image correlation (HR-DIC) [ 7 ] or using synchrotron X-ray data to find grain-averaged stresses [ 8 ,  9 ,  10 ,  11 ,  12 ,  13 ,  14 – 15 ].

A more detailed method for finding 3D grain morphologies can be achieved through the use of EBSD and serial sectioning. Signor et al. [ 22 ] and Diehl et al. [ 23 ] used mechanical polishing to remove thin layers of material and subsequently take EBSD images of the newly exposed surface. Stacking these layers gives an exact view of the 3D microstructure which is only limited by the resolution of the EBSD data set. 3D EBSD can also be performed using a focused ion beam (FIB) to mill away precise layers of material [ 24 ] as opposed to the more approximate mechanical polishing route.

Hestroffer [ 25 ] used high-resolution 3D EBSD in conjunction with crystal plasticity finite element to recreate the 3D microstructure of the nickel-based superalloy IN718. This paper explored the impact of a columnar grain representation versus the full 3D model and found significant differences between the modelling approaches, highlighting the high sensitivity of the mesoscale mechanical behaviour to the sub-surface microstructure.

sections.heading: Elevated temperature, in situ HR-EBSD tensile test
paragraphs: A detailed description of the experiment performed within this work is presented in [ 26 ], so only a summary will be provided here.

One side of an AISI 316 H stainless steel dog-bone with the geometry shown in Fig.  1 a was metallographically prepared to ensure high-quality high-angular-resolution electron backscatter diffraction (HR-EBSD) patterns. The final step of the process involved using a suspension of 0.05 µm colloidal silica on a VibroMet 2 vibro-polisher. Figure 1 a  Sample geometry,  b  Large EBSD map collected,  c  Loading curve.

sections.heading: HR-EBSD analysis
paragraphs: It is possible to extract type-III elastic strain information from HR-EBSD maps using the commercial software package CrossCourt4 [ 27 ], which uses a Kikuchi pattern cross-correlation technique described in [ 27 ,  28 – 29 ].

This method functions by comparing every Kikuchi pattern within a grain to a single reference pattern which is assumed to have zero strain; however, finding this zero strain pattern represents a considerable challenge. A few different approaches have been proposed to find this zero strain pattern [ 30 ,  31 ,  32 – 33 ], with CrossCourt4 suggesting that the kernel average misorientation (KAM) is able to give a good approximation of a zero strain location.

Within this work, the minimum KAM is used as the indicator for a zero strain pattern due to this being available within the commercial software. As a result of this choice, it should be noted that any strains reported with this work are not absolute, but instead are relative to the software-decided zero strain pattern in each grain.

sections.heading: Comparing HR-EBSD patterns at different loading strains
paragraphs: Previous work by Deal et al. [ 34 ] used EBSD patterns of similarly oriented annealed grains in a titanium alloy with strained material to obtain a better representation of zero strain EBSD patterns. This work follows a similar process for collecting a strain free map by using reference patterns from the pre-test HR-EBSD map at every loading step. By taking this approach, an improved indication of intragranular elastic strain evolution with respect to loading strain can be achieved. This improved strain evolution data can be seen in Fig.  2 , which shows the strain predicted in one grain when using a single pattern from a pre-test map and when using a different pattern for each loading step. Figure 2 Average elastic strain in one grain (shown in  a ) varying with loading strain when using a single pattern (red x) and multiple patterns (black dot).

sections.heading: fs laser 3D EBSD of tensile test specimen
paragraphs: After the in situ tensile experiment, the specimen was cut close to the region analysed with HR-EBSD using electrical discharge machining. Prior to machining, the HR-EBSD region was identified and protected with ion beam deposited platinum using a Thermo Fisher Scientific Helios 5 fs laser Plasma FIB (L-PFIB) system. Subsequently, an abrasive silicon carbide disc was used to grind down the cut face until the edge of the HR-EBSD area was around 300 µm from this face. To ensure the sample had the correct thickness that the fs laser could cut through, the back of the specimen was ground down using a Metaverse grinding machine until it was 500 µm thick. Figure  3 a and b shows the original specimen and the final geometry before the fs laser, receptively. The remainder of the sample preparation and subsequent serial sectioning took place back in the Thermo Fisher Scientific Helios 5 Laser-PFIB system which was also fitted with an Oxford Instruments Symmetry EBSD detector. Figure 3 Figure of the specimen with sectioning plane shown  b  Diagram of the specimen post-sample preparation.  c  The 3D EBSD fib section under the SEM after the bulk milling operation.

Upon collection of the data, the fs laser was used to cut away 1.5 µm of the block from the front face. The polishing, imaging, and slicing steps were repeated until the entire 700-µm block had been cut away and imaged. Each cycle took 9 min 30 s to collect (1m02s laser slice, 1m28s ion beam polishing, 1m12s EBSD acquisition, and the balance stage movements, image acquisitions, and detector insertion/retraction) The total experiment, of 432 slices, took roughly 69 h. The final, reconstructed 3D EBSD data set collected is visible in Fig.  4 . Figure 4 3D EBSD data set after reconstruction. The area monitored during the tensile test described in Section “ Methods ” is indicated.

sections.heading: Crystal plasticity model
paragraphs: The crystal plasticity model used within this work is based on a large strain framework initially suggested by Kalidindi et al. [ 35 ]. For a detailed description of the time integration scheme used, please refer to [ 35 ].

sections.heading: Constitutive laws
Calibration
CPFE model geometries and boundary conditions
paragraphs: To explore the influence of sub-surface microstructure, two different geometries were created.

sections.heading: 3D simulation
paragraphs: Once the geometry was created, symmetry boundary conditions were applied to three sides, labelled A, B, and C in Fig.  6 c. The displacement applied during the experiment was applied to the right side in the same increments as seen experimentally.

sections.heading: Oligocrystal simulation
paragraphs: The same boundary conditions were applied to the oligocrystal as to the 3D model, with symmetry being applied to sides A, B, and C and the loading seen experimentally being applied to the right face. The final geometry and boundary conditions are displayed in Figure  6 b and c, respectively. The oligocrystal model did not contain any sub-surface microstructure from the experiment, so when comparing its results to the 3D model, analysis of the influence of the sub-surface microstructure was possible.
The oligocrystal used the same calibrated parameters as the 3D EBSD simulation.

sections.heading: Differences between the 3D model and the oligocrystal
paragraphs: This work aims to provide an indication as to the influence of the sub-surface microstructure. The oligocrystal (Fig.  6 b) represents a case in which the sub-surface microstructure is not available for experiments so only the surface can be modelled accurately. The 3D model allows for the full 3D microstructure to be represented (Fig.  6 a). The applied boundary conditions are the same in both models so by comparing the mechanical behaviour of the two simulations, it is possible to determine how influential the sub-surface microstructure is. This will provide an insight as to what data are required to accurately reproduce 1:1 mesoscale mechanical behaviour.

sections.heading: Bulk deformation behaviour
paragraphs: An initial assessment into the mechanical behaviour of the two simulations was performed by extracting the bulk response of each volume. This is shown in Fig.  7  via a set of stress strain curves. Both models show a similar response, despite the using same calibration (see Table  1 ) and their microstructural differences. This matches the bulk experimental response, indicating the models are representative of the averaged behaviour. The experiment shown in Fig.  7  is taken from work by Allen et al. [ 52 ], which used the same 316 H cast (ELG) and temperature as that used in this work. The slight variation in the 3D EBSD and the oligocrystal stress–strain curves are due to the microstructural variation between the two simulations. The 3D EBSD structure has a different set of grains (and so orientations) under the surface compared to the oligocrystal so the mechanical response is slightly different. Figure 7 Bulk deformation loading curves for the two simulations and an experiment on the same material at the same temperature.

sections.heading: Elastic strain evolution
paragraphs: Whilst this initial qualitative analysis provides some insight, it is possible to obtain quantitative values of the strain profiles. A line profile, visible in Fig.  9 g, was used to compare the two models with each other. Figure 9 Elastic strain along the line shown in  g  for both models. The blue section is analysed in Fig.  10 .

sections.heading: Singular grain response over time
paragraphs: From the experiment described in Section “ Methods ”, the evolution of elastic strain over time within the small area of interest was captured by performing HR-EBSD scans at specified strains. Using this information, the average change in elastic strain per grain was extracted. The same elastic strain response over time was also extracted from the two models outlined above so it is possible to compare the experiment with the model results. In the raw experimental data, the elastic strain does not start at exactly zero due to the lack of an absolute zero strain pattern as well as any strain that may have been retained from manufacturing. To account for this unknown, the work performed focuses on the strain evolution over time rather than the absolute values.

Examining the evolution of strain over time is more meaningful when all the data being compared starts at zero due to uncertainty in the zero stress state of the grains. So, to achieve this, the experimental data are shifted so that the strain at the beginning of the test is zero in every component. Figure  10  presents the average change in elastic strain of all stress components within the grain highlighted in Fig.  10 g for the two models as well as the experiment. Figure 10 Elastic strain response over time of the models and experiment for every strain component. The grain analysed in highlighted in  g .

sections.heading: Texture evolution
paragraphs: In addition to considering the elastic stress, the EBSD data collected enable the comparison of local orientation changes within each grain. The CPFE code utilized is also able to output local orientation changes so experiment and model can be compared using this metric.

sections.heading: Inverse pole figure
paragraphs: Figure 12 Post-test inverse pole figure Z plots of the experiment  a , the oligocrystal simulation  b , and the 3D simulation  c .

Figure  12  shows a comparison on the Z-inverse pole figure plots from the oligocrystal, the 3D EBSD mesh, and the experiment after loading. Whilst all three IPF plots resemble each other to an extent, due to them all starting with the same spatially resolved orientation distribution, the local texture changes due to the deformation in the experiment do not match well with either model. The 3D EBSD simulation shows a wider spread, which more closely resembles the experimental data in magnitude.

sections.heading: Grain reference orientation deviation
paragraphs: To enable comparisons between experiment and modelling when looking at local changes in texture, the grain reference orientation deviation (GROD) was used. In this method, the mean orientation of each grain is found and the misorientation between this mean value and the orientation at each data point within the desired mesh is calculated. GROD is better able to show broad changes in orientation across a grain compared to other local misorientation measures such as lattice curvature. This ability to pick up broad changes means that GROD has less dependence on the resolution and mesh size, which leads to significant advantages with respect to CPFE modelling, because this allows for validation of models to be performed with coarser meshes.

Figure  13  shows the contour maps of the GROD in the experiment (Fig.  13 a) and the two models (Fig.  13 b, c) When comparing between model results, the GROD contour maps give further evidence as to the lesser local change in orientation seen in the oligocrystal compared to the 3D EBSD model. All three contour plots show larger orientation changes towards grain boundaries, which is expected because plastic deformation will primarily occur in these locations and the local orientation shifts can be interpreted as an indicator of plasticity. Figure 13 Grain reference orientation deviation contour maps in  a  the experiment,  b  the oligocrystal model, and  c  the 3D EBSD model.

A quantitative comparison between experiment and model is shown in Fig.  14  by taking line profiles at various locations on the free surface of the sample/model. These locations are shown in Fig.  14 a. It is evident that along line 1, the oligocrystal shows significantly less misorientation compared to both the 3D EBSD and experiment, whilst the 3D EBSD model and experimental data follow similar general trends and magnitudes. The 3D EBSD model shows less fit with the experimental data in Fig.  14 c, but still follows the same general trend. The oligocrystal sees greater magnitudes along line 2 than line 1, but these still are often lower than the experiment. Figure 14 Line profiles at various positions shown in  a .  b – c  are the line profiles.

Whilst Fig.  14  indicates more similarities between the experiment and 3D EBSD model, a comparison between Fig.  13 a and c clearly shows that not every grain gives similar orientation distributions.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The work presented in this paper investigates the influence of the sub-surface microstructure on intragranular deformation and leads to the conclusion that even if the bulk behaviour is similar between models, the local behaviour may vary significantly.

Whilst Fig.  7  indicates that the bulk response was similar in the two models, Fig.  8  shows that the intragranular response differed. This difference was further corroborated by Fig.  10 , which suggested that the change in strain over time in the grain examined was different between the two models. These three figures together give an initial indication as to the importance of the sub-surface microstructure; however, when the experimental data were compared to the model, it was found that there was limited matching between elastic strains.

Mclean et al. [ 31 ] explored nano-scale complex geometries undergoing bi-axial loading conditions, which were used to validate the cross-correlation approach. This work showed good agreement for normal and in-plane measurements, but there was less agreement for out-of-plane components. The authors suggested that small mis-alignments during measurement and loading could cause substantial errors in out-of-plane measurements, so these should not be relied upon. Mclean et al.’s conclusions fit with the results seen in this work, so the out-of-plane experimental measurements are be assumed to be inaccurate for the same reasons. In addition to Mclean et al.’s work, Andani et al. [ 45 ] and Tong [ 54 ] also looked at in-plane stresses at grain boundaries using the cross-correlation technique and found that it presented acceptable results, giving further evidence to the technique’s ability to measure in-plane strains.

In addition to the elastic strain, the local orientation changes were analysed. Figure  12  indicates that the local orientation changes were different between the two models, which further indicated the importance of the sub-surface microstructure. The inclusion of the experimental IPF-Z plot showed that, whilst neither model texture maps give an exact match, the 3D EBSD information showed more similarities in terms of spread than the oligocrystal model.

For an in-depth comparison of the spatially resolved local orientation changes, the GROD was utilized because the method is less step-size-dependent compared to a measure such as kernel average misorientation (KAM) or lattice curvature. This was important within this analysis because the model geometry had a different element size than the step size used in the experiment meaning that the measured KAM would not be directly comparable. Figure  13  presents the GROD contour maps, which further backs the observation of the previous two figures that showed that the oligocrystal experiences significantly less change in local orientation over time. Additionally, Fig.  14  indicates that the 3D model shows good agreement with the experimentally calculated GROD in some grains, whilst the oligocrystal does not. This is an interesting observation because it means that local texture evolution on the free surface is greatly influenced by the sub-surface microstructure and, as such, is necessary to correctly predict local deformation.

Another possible reason for mismatch between experiment and model in Fig.  14  comes from the change in grain morphology during loading. This leads to any line profile extracted not following the exact same path in the model and experiment so differences in results become apparent. The small applied strain limits this uncertainty as only limited grain deformation occurs, but there will still be some effect, especially when comparing high-resolution images.

Whilst the CPFE model presented showed some similarities to the experimental data, some limitations and assumptions are present within this work. One such assumption was that the loading was uniform and only occurred on one face. In reality, the anisotropic nature of the microstructure would have produced a non-uniform displacement on the area simulated. This would likely change intragranular interactions, particularly at the boundaries of the model, and so lead to a different behaviour in some areas. The exact displacements experienced by the geometry were not available because keeping track of individual locations and their respective movements between EBSD maps is a significant challenge that was out of the scope of this research. One method that allows for tracking displacements at the nano-scale is high-resolution digital image correlation (HR-DIC). Alongside this, HR-DIC can provide information about total intragranular strain, so is a good tool for validating model results whilst also providing accurate displacement information. Multiple authors have demonstrated that validation is possible with this technique [ 4 ,  7 ,  60 ,  61 ] so this seems a clear path for future demonstration of CPFE’s abilities.

A further limitation of the work presented is the use of the post-test microstructure to construct the mesh. This did not have a significant impact due to the small total strain applied, but still represents a possible improvement that could be applied to this work. Various methods exist for capturing the pre-test microstructure of a sample, such as near-field XRD [ 62 ], diffraction contrast tomography [ 63 ], and 3D XRD [ 64 ,  65 ]; however, these techniques are either too low resolution or prohibitively complex and expensive for the minor improvements they may make.

The current model used within this work has shown to be able to predict the correct slip systems activating (see Horton et al. [ 26 ]), but the use of a single latent hardening value may not be sufficient for intragranular predictions. One possibility to overcome this is by using the Wu and Bassani [ 70 ] latent hardening, which is designed to specifically account for the sequential slip system activation seen in FCC crystals. To accompany this, Lin et al. [ 71 ] compared multiple latent hardening rules and found that Wu and Bassani represented the best approximation.

Attempting to directly replicate a micrsotructure 1-to-1 allows for a straight forward comparison between the experiment and the simulations, so is a good fit for model validation, as has been carried out in this paper. This method shines when there is lots of detailed data available about a small area of microstructure. This allows for investigation and validation of the minutiae of individual grains, such as slip system activation, local orientation changes, and intragranular stress distributions. If large amounts of data are available, with varying levels of quality, the use of statistical techniques such as pseudorandom 3D grain-scale modelling [ 72 ] can be used for validation, because they are able to capture the general behaviour in many different, but statistically similar microstructures. The primary downside of pseudorandom grain-scale modelling is the need for a statically representative amount of microstructural information, which can be expensive to acquire and so limit its use.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In this paper, the effect of the sub-surface microstructure on mechanical behaviour was investigated. To provide a comprehensive analysis, evolution of both elastic strains and crystallographic orientations was considered. The following conclusions were found as a result of this work. When comparing the 3D EBSD and oligocrystal models, a similar response was predicted in the bulk material, but different behaviour was predicted within each grain. The model-predicted in-plane elastic strains in some components matched with the experimental data. When considering local orientation changes, the 3D EBSD model generally showed a better match with the experiment than the oligocrystal model. The above bullet points lead to the conclusion that the sub-surface structure is important if the correct local behaviour is to be modelled.
